title: Letter 29 — Be Faithful unto Death
attribution_note: Letter 29 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: A good beginning needs a good end

pairs.en: Though I neither know you nor have seen you, yet I have heard who you are and whence you came, and how you entered into your calling. A good beginning! O that the end might be good as well — without which the beginning is nothing! For not the beginning and the middle, but the end is praised, and completes the whole work, according to Christ's word: *“Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.”* [Revelation 2:10]

I have heard that it is hard for you because of the hatred and malice of those who dwell with you, and that you wish to leave that place and go to one of the monasteries of Moscow. If truly men hate you and do you evil, this is the snare of the devil, who stirs up the hatred and malice of men against a pious soul, that he may cast her down and turn her aside from the good way. And the poor people who hate a pious soul and do her evil know not themselves what they do; for it happens that afterward they repent and grieve for it.

Therefore lay the blame of your affliction also upon this our enemy of souls, and forgive men, and pray for them. Yield not to your adversary, and stand in your former place, as a brave soldier stands against his adversary and gives him no ground. Stand you also, and yield not to him, that he may not rejoice over you. Know for certain that wherever you may be, everywhere he will trouble you through men and through himself. You will live in quietness and have good rest, if you endure with silence and without murmuring all that befalls you from him himself and from men.

To a pious soul living in this world, everywhere is a foreign land, and everywhere unrest, until she goes to her heavenly Fatherland. There she will rest sweetly after her labours and her struggle — and that forever, not for a time. But even here, in this world, if you would have any rest, you can find it nowhere, if you cannot have patience.

Therefore give yourself over to patience, and you will have rest within yourself, though they trouble you much from without. Let men call you what they will, let them say of you what they will; but look into the mirror of your conscience, and take comfort in its witness, and look toward the glory to come, which is prepared for them that endure.
All that is temporal will pass away, though it be very bitter and long-lasting; but eternal glory and blessedness never pass away.

sections.heading: Follow Christ and keep your vows

pairs.en: Look upon Christ: what did He not endure for us? Look upon the saints: did not they all follow Christ by faith and by patience? And with what shall we appear there before them, if we will not endure here? What mark shall we show that we are Christians, if we will not bear the cross and follow Christ by patience? Shall we show only this — that we live in monasteries and wear black garments? We must take care lest this very thing accuse us there.

The monastic life and the black garment — these are humility and repentance; but if we will not follow Christ, who humbled Himself for our sake, then where are our vows, by which at Baptism we promised to serve Christ? Where are the vows which we repeated at our tonsure, and promised to have humility, obedience, patience, meekness and the rest?

Is a man a monk only until he is tonsured? Do the black robe and the vows make the monk, and not the deed itself? No, no!.. Of all Christians it is required that they go by the narrow and strait way; but especially of the monk and of nuns. Who persuaded us to shut ourselves in a monastery and wear black garments, and endure straitness and sorrow? We ourselves chose it. Why then should we flee from what we ourselves have chosen? All Christians who are remiss will be without answer at the dread Judgment of Christ, but especially monks and nuns who keep not their vows.

Remember all this, beloved, and go not out of the monastery in which you are, but endure all things, that you may receive the crown of life. There is no crown without victory, no victory without struggle, no struggle without battle, no battle without enemies.

Therefore one must fight, strive, and conquer by patience, that one may be crowned by the Captain of the contest, Jesus Christ. Therefore if you have begun to be a soldier of Christ, so remain unto the end: then will Christ own you as His soldier, and give *“thee a crown of life,”* and you will be blessed forever.

Christian victory consists in nothing other than manful patience under sorrows and assaults. There is no more glorious victory than to conquer one's own anger and oneself. But if you have a legitimate cause to leave this monastery, then even so go not to the monasteries of Moscow, but go to some monastery elsewhere and live there. Only I assure you that the devil will trouble you everywhere. The Lord keep us from him!
Your well-wisher, Tikhon, former bishop of Voronezh.
